nodes.label: Two-generator-tree byte-identity guard
nodes.rationale: `nova new` (templateFS) and `nova add` (skelFS) deliberately keep separate template trees, so the cmd/worker.go and internal/app/worker.go they emit can silently drift. The tests render both from the same {ModuleName} data and assert byte equality, converting drift into a test failure instead of two divergent worker bootstraps.

nodes.label: Nova working principles (think first, simplicity, surgical, goal-driven)
nodes.rationale: Adapted from karpathy-style skills to bias toward caution over speed: state assumptions, ship the minimum, keep every changed line traceable to the request, and turn the task into a verifiable goal (make lint + make test green, matrix case added in the same change).
nodes.norm_label: nova working principles (think first, simplicity, surgical, goal-driven)

nodes.label: embed.FS + text/template rendering strategy
nodes.rationale: All framework/DB variants coexist in one embedded template tree; buildFileList() selects files by `cond` booleans so a single binary can render any stack without shipping per-stack template sets.

nodes.label: Variant-prefixed template naming convention
nodes.rationale: `{fiber,gin,chi,echo}_handler.go.tmpl` -> handler.go lets every variant live side by side and be picked at render time from cfg. Adding a framework/engine therefore requires BOTH the prefixed files and an extension of the whitelist in generator.New(), which validates before any template path is resolved.

nodes.label: ProjectConfig as single source of truth
nodes.rationale: Templates and buildFileList() both condition on ProjectConfig's boolean helpers (HasHTTP, HasSQL, UseWire, ...), so a new capability is added as one helper rather than duplicated predicates in two places.
nodes.norm_label: projectconfig as single source of truth

nodes.label: Component layout manifest for `nova add`
nodes.rationale: `nova new` and `nova add` are independent generators with different template trees; `add` decides WHERE files go via the manifest so it works in projects nova did not generate. Default() declares more layout keys (cache/grpc/publisher/migration/query) than have generators, so a nova.yaml can describe them ahead of implementation.

nodes.label: skel/ tree — one directory per `add` command
nodes.rationale: Keeping `add`'s templates in skel/ (embedded via skelFS) separate from the `nova new` tree means the two generators evolve independently; a new template-driven command is a new directory plus a []renderSpec.
nodes.norm_label: skel/ tree — one directory per `add` command

nodes.label: GenerateWorker scaffolds a runnable worker service
nodes.rationale: The worker is the one `add` command that emits entry points and touches DI: app/worker.go boots through di.InitializeWorker so it stays broker-agnostic and byte-identical to `nova new`'s template (pinned by TestWorkerAppTemplatesIdentical); each DI symbol is written only when diPkgDeclares says the package lacks it, so re-runs never duplicate and worker-enabled projects are untouched; shared transport files use skipIfExists so a second `add worker` only appends its feature handler.
nodes.norm_label: generateworker scaffolds a runnable worker service

nodes.label: sqlc repository generator is field-driven code-gen, not a template
nodes.rationale: GenerateRepository delegates to repository_sqlc.go, which AST-parses the existing entity and maps each field per engine, so the emitted impl matches `nova new`'s hand-written repository but parameterized by real fields. The entity MUST exist first because it supplies the columns; this is also why GenerateEntity emits a typed port (*entity.X) — the generated impl has to satisfy it.
nodes.norm_label: sqlc repository generator is field-driven code-gen, not a template

nodes.label: Nova design docs (index)
nodes.rationale: These are the design reference for what `nova new` GENERATES, not CLI docs; docs 05-12 are a pattern reference (not an inventory), and several documented layers — domain/valueobject, domain/service, domain/event, adapter/external, transport/cronjob — are deliberately not scaffolded today.

nodes.label: Where doc and template disagree, the template wins
nodes.rationale: Naming one side authoritative removes the ambiguity of a mismatch: the doc is the bug and gets fixed in the same change, so docs can't silently become an alternative spec.
nodes.norm_label: where doc and template disagree, the template wins

nodes.label: Usecase layer (Layer 2)
nodes.rationale: A usecase orchestrates: loads entities through ports, applies application policy, performs side effects, returns its own DTOs. Entities never cross this boundary — transport only ever sees usecase Output types.

nodes.label: Usecase error discipline: errors.L vs errors.Wrapf
nodes.rationale: A rule the caller violated becomes errors.L (translatable code + HTTP status); a failed dependency becomes errors.Wrapf (caller frame + context, cause preserved). The service never logs — it wraps and returns so the transport boundary logs exactly once per request instead of once per layer.
nodes.norm_label: usecase error discipline: errors.l vs errors.wrapf

nodes.label: Register — switch on the lookup error
nodes.rationale: Only ErrNotFound means 'free to create'. Collapsing the switch to `if err != nil { proceed }` turns a database outage into a duplicate insert. The uniqueness check is advisory — it only buys the friendly UserEmailExists message; the UNIQUE constraint in the migration is the real guarantee, and two concurrent registers can both pass the check.
nodes.norm_label: register — switch on the lookup error

nodes.label: Best-effort event publish (the one place a service logs)
nodes.rationale: The user is already persisted, so a broker outage must not fail the request; but an error that is never returned must be logged somewhere or it vanishes. Guaranteed delivery is an outbox row written in the same transaction, not a retry loop here.
nodes.norm_label: best-effort event publish (the one place a service logs)

nodes.label: List — pagination policy clamped in the usecase
nodes.rationale: Defaults and caps live in the usecase so every transport (HTTP, gRPC, CLI) inherits one policy, and ListOutput echoes the CLAMPED values so the page meta the client sees matches what was actually queried.
nodes.norm_label: list — pagination policy clamped in the usecase

nodes.label: PublicList — cursor (keyset) paging
nodes.rationale: limit+1 rows reveal HasMore without a second query; keyset (id > cursor) is stable under concurrent inserts and avoids deep-OFFSET scans; the cursor is base64 opaque but not secret; the projection is email+name only so an anonymous caller learns nothing more; a malformed cursor is a 400 because the client returned a token we issued.

nodes.label: Login — uniform failure AND uniform timing
nodes.rationale: Equal status is the easy half. bcrypt is CPU-bound, so an unknown user would return in microseconds while a wrong password takes ~100ms — a reliable enumeration oracle even with identical bodies. The not-found path therefore verifies against a sync.Once-primed dummy hash so wall-clock time matches.
nodes.norm_label: login — uniform failure and uniform timing

nodes.label: Usecase package `svc` import alias
nodes.rationale: The usecase package and the transport package for a feature are both named after the aggregate (package user), so call sites always import the usecase as usersvc/ordersvc — never the bare name.

nodes.label: Filter passthrough rule (do you need a usecase DTO?)
nodes.rationale: If the usecase does zero transformation, the transport assembler can build the domain filter directly and the DTO is dead weight. The shipped List earns ListInput because it clamps.
nodes.norm_label: filter passthrough rule (do you need a usecase dto?)

nodes.label: Domain service interfaces in domain/, implementations in usecase/
nodes.rationale: A domain service is pure business logic with no external system behind it, so its implementation is not an adapter. It is injected into other usecases and never called from a handler — a handler calling it directly skips the orchestration layer.
nodes.norm_label: domain service interfaces in domain/, implementations in usecase/

nodes.label: Repository vs domain service vs usecase decision table
nodes.rationale: Rule of thumb: returns data (even a 10-table JOIN) -> repository; returns a decision/computation over multiple entities with no I/O -> domain service; orchestrates steps with side effects -> use case.
nodes.norm_label: repository vs domain service vs usecase decision table

nodes.label: Transport layer (inbound delivery)
nodes.rationale: A sibling of adapter/, not a child. Transports are mutually exclusive in a generated project: one --transport flag, one of http/grpc/worker.

nodes.label: Middleware order is load-bearing
nodes.rationale: RequestID first so every later layer including the logger sees the ID; Logging second so it wraps everything and can emit one line with a duration; Recovery inside Logging so a panic still produces an access log; CORS after observability; Locale last so WriteError can read the language back. /healthz and /readyz are mounted INSIDE the stack so a panic during a readiness check still returns the envelope.

nodes.label: Registrar interface + deterministic slice mount order
nodes.rationale: registrars is a slice, not a map: map iteration order would make route shadowing nondeterministic between restarts. Prefix is mounted as a subgroup before Register is called, so multiple registrars can share a prefix.
nodes.norm_label: registrar interface + deterministic slice mount order

nodes.label: v1.Prefixed — the shared /api/v1 prefix by embedding
nodes.rationale: Declaring APIPrefix once per API section and supplying Prefix() via embedding means no feature restates the prefix; a new section (/admin, /api/v2) is a sibling package with its own APIPrefix and Prefixed base.
nodes.norm_label: v1.prefixed — the shared /api/v1 prefix by embedding

nodes.label: Per-feature transport package (dto/assembler/handler/registrar)
nodes.rationale: A flat v1/ with request.go/response.go/user_handler.go/order_handler.go becomes unmanageable at 10+ features. Per-feature keeps one endpoint group in one package, and deleting a feature is deleting a directory.

nodes.label: One DTO, every framework (dual query:/form: tags)
nodes.rationale: dto.go and assembler.go are the only feature files with no framework variant; carrying both query: (fiber, echo) and form: (gin) tags is what buys that. Validation here is shape (formats, enums), never policy — magnitude caps belong to the usecase so gRPC/CLI inherit them.
nodes.norm_label: one dto, every framework (dual query:/form: tags)

nodes.label: assembler.go — the only place that maps (usecase -> wire)
nodes.rationale: Data and meta get separate projections because the envelope keeps them in separate fields and the two list shapes produce different meta types. tokenType "Bearer" is a wire-format constant so it lives here, not in the usecase output. There is no request->input assembler: two-field mappings do not earn a named function.
nodes.norm_label: assembler.go — the only place that maps (usecase -> wire)

nodes.label: Handlers never log — WriteError is the single funnel
nodes.rationale: Every error passes through httpwriter.WriteError, which stashes the AppError in ctx; the Logging middleware picks it up after the handler returns. One funnel is the only place that can hand the error to logging, which is what makes one-line-per-request achievable without a log call in the handler.
nodes.norm_label: handlers never log — writeerror is the single funnel

nodes.label: Fiber: c.UserContext(), never c.Context()
nodes.rationale: c.Context() is the fasthttp request context; the context.Context carrying request ID, logger, locale and principal is UserContext(). Passing the wrong one silently drops all of it — no error, just missing correlation.

nodes.label: Auth applied at the route group, not per route
nodes.rationale: One Auth middleware instance for the whole protected subtree makes the boundary visible in four lines, and a newly added protected route cannot forget it. tokenSvc and loginLimit arrive via the constructor so the registrar is testable and limiter state is per-instance, not a package global.
nodes.norm_label: auth applied at the route group, not per route

nodes.label: Binders collapse every failure to one generic localized 400
nodes.rationale: Uniform messages stop a client probing struct field names or binder internals; WithCause keeps the real field failure in the access log's app_err/app_trace, correlated by request_id. Per-field errors in the response would be a deliberate change to ErrorResponseFromApp, not a patch here.
nodes.norm_label: binders collapse every failure to one generic localized 400

nodes.label: Liveness vs readiness split
nodes.rationale: Liveness is a no-op success — answering the request IS the signal. Coupling it to DB or cache health means a database blip restarts every healthy pod, turning a degradation into an outage. Readiness pings dependencies under a 1s deadline and reports a per-check details map so an operator sees which one is down.

nodes.label: Worker ack decision: poison message acks, failed downstream nacks
nodes.rationale: Malformed JSON will fail identically forever and on Kafka blocks the partition, so it is logged and acked; a failed downstream is transient so the error is returned to trigger nack/retry. Getting this backwards is the classic worker outage — a poison message parked at the head of a partition.
nodes.norm_label: worker ack decision: poison message acks, failed downstream nacks

nodes.label: Topic constant deliberately duplicated on both sides
nodes.rationale: A shared constant would couple the consumer's module to the producer's — fine in one repo, wrong the moment the worker becomes a separate service. The duplication carries a comment pointing at its twin instead.
nodes.norm_label: topic constant deliberately duplicated on both sides

nodes.label: The full locale flow (header -> ctx -> translated envelope)
nodes.rationale: The status is decided when the error is CREATED (errors.L looks the code up in localeHTTPStatus), not at the boundary — that is what lets a gRPC or worker transport reuse the same classification without duplicating a status table. The usecase never imports a translation file or learns the caller's language.
nodes.norm_label: the full locale flow (header -> ctx -> translated envelope)

nodes.label: Per-IP token bucket on /login only
nodes.rationale: In-process, so N replicas means N x the limit: it raises the cost of credential stuffing, it is not an edge WAF. Global shedding belongs upstream where it can drop traffic before it reaches the app; the visitors map grows with distinct IPs and wants an LRU if /login sees high-cardinality traffic.

nodes.label: gRPC transport is a compiling placeholder
nodes.rationale: Server bootstrap, DI graph and entry point are real; only the service implementation is left to the user. interceptor/ is the gRPC counterpart to HTTP middleware and cannot share a package with it.
nodes.norm_label: grpc transport is a compiling placeholder

nodes.label: Adapter layer (Layer 3)
nodes.rationale: An adapter fulfils a domain port by talking to an external system. Anything that merely CREATES the client is infrastructure.

nodes.label: The three-file SQL repository (tx_manager + qx + repository)
nodes.rationale: Split so no file does two jobs, and to solve one problem: a repository method must join an ambient transaction without knowing whether one is running. The usecase says WithinTx; every repository call inside silently uses that transaction.
nodes.norm_label: the three-file sql repository (tx_manager + qx + repository)

nodes.label: TxManager.WithinTx — unconditional rollback, nesting reuses
nodes.rationale: defer Rollback is unconditional (a post-commit rollback is a discarded no-op) so no path — not even a panic in fn — leaks a connection. WithinTx inside WithinTx reuses the ambient tx rather than opening a second one, so composing two usecase methods cannot deadlock against itself; genuine nesting would be savepoints. txKey is an unexported zero-size type so no other package can collide or read the tx out.

nodes.label: qx — the TX-aware query executor
nodes.rationale: base is built once so the common non-transactional path allocates nothing. Type and constructor are unexported and qx is held as a field rather than embedded — embedding would promote Q onto the repository's public method set. The constructor takes the pool so DI never learns qx exists.

nodes.label: Driver sentinel -> domain sentinel translation
nodes.rationale: Translating pgx.ErrNoRows (or sql.ErrNoRows) into errors.ErrNotFound is the whole reason this is an adapter and not infrastructure: a driver sentinel is a storage detail, and the usecase checks errors.Is(err, errors.ErrNotFound) and stays portable across engines.

nodes.label: mapper/ — pure row <-> entity functions
nodes.rationale: No DB handles, no context, one file per entity — so mapping is unit-testable with no database and the repository file stays readable. It is also where the storage-vs-domain naming gap is absorbed (column `password` -> field PasswordHash) and where pgtype.Timestamptz is confined so it never escapes the package.

nodes.label: sqlc reads migrations as its schema source
nodes.rationale: schema: ["migrations"] means exactly one definition of the tables; a separate schema.sql is a second source of truth that drifts. The jsonb -> json.RawMessage override keeps payload columns as raw bytes so the mapper doesn't re-encode them.
nodes.norm_label: sqlc reads migrations as its schema source

nodes.label: Optional filters as one prepared statement (sqlc.arg idiom)
nodes.rationale: `sqlc.arg('email') = '' OR email = ...` keeps an optional filter in a single prepared statement: no string concatenation, no injection surface, one query plan. Named args give readable Params field names and let CountUsers share the filter while ignoring limit/offset. SELECT * is safe because sqlc regenerates the row struct from the migration.
nodes.norm_label: optional filters as one prepared statement (sqlc.arg idiom)

nodes.label: Known bug: `nova new` migration emits postgres DDL for mysql
nodes.rationale: create_users_table ships BIGSERIAL / TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE even for --database=mysql. `nova add repository` does emit correct per-engine DDL via repository_sqlc.go, so the two generators disagree.
nodes.norm_label: known bug: `nova new` migration emits postgres ddl for mysql

nodes.label: Publisher split so swapping brokers touches one file
nodes.rationale: Wire DTOs own the json tags and domain events have none, so renaming a JSON field is a wire-format change that cannot reach the domain. Only publisher.go is broker-specific and its exported surface is identical per broker, so DI never changes when the broker does.
nodes.norm_label: publisher split so swapping brokers touches one file

nodes.label: Redis cache-aside decorator over UserRepository
nodes.rationale: Three deliberate asymmetries: read failures degrade to the database but a failed DEL after a write returns an error (a stale entry is worse than a retryable request); GetByEmail never caches because it is the login path that needs the hash, and the cached projection omits credentials; List/Count/ListAfter don't cache because any write invalidates every page. Not wired by default — where caching is correct is a domain decision.

nodes.label: Elasticsearch adapter as a derived read model
nodes.rationale: Not a decorator: the SQL repository stays the system of record and the index is derived state. Search returns IDs you hydrate through SQL, so the index can never serve stale field values; the doc projection is id+name+email only. Not wired by default because enabling it means accepting the write-path consistency burden.
nodes.norm_label: elasticsearch adapter as a derived read model

nodes.label: Two ports satisfied outside adapter/
nodes.rationale: Satisfying a port is necessary but not sufficient for adapter/: PasswordHasher is pure computation and Logger is cross-cutting, so both live in infrastructure/ instead.

nodes.label: Infrastructure layer (Layer 4)
nodes.rationale: Technical capabilities, no business logic. The test: creates a client/pool/producer -> infrastructure; uses that client to fulfil a domain port -> adapter; translates a driver error into a domain error -> adapter; satisfies a port with pure computation -> infrastructure.

nodes.label: The (instance, cleanup, error) constructor contract
nodes.rationale: Each component owns its own shutdown — no Close() on a domain port, no central teardown listing every resource. Adding a dependency therefore cannot leak it: if it needs teardown its constructor returns the hook and the DI graph picks it up. Constructors also verify connectivity (ping/declare) so a misconfigured dependency fails at startup, not on the first production request.

nodes.label: Config precedence: base.yaml -> <APP_ENV>.yaml -> env vars
nodes.rationale: YAML is //go:embed-ed so Load() takes no path and the binary has no cwd dependency — the cost is that a config change is a rebuild, the intended trade for a service image. The YAML/.env split is by NATURE not convenience: operational tuning is reviewed in code review, secrets and per-deploy endpoints are injected, which is why JWT keys carry only an env: tag. APP_ENV is whitelisted, so a typo silently gets base defaults rather than a missing-file error.

nodes.label: Sub-config projection (consumers take the sub-struct)
nodes.rationale: A component's signature then documents exactly what it reads and no constructor can quietly start depending on an unrelated section. NewRouter is the one exception because it configures the framework from HTTP and branches on AppEnv.

nodes.label: CORS default rejects all cross-origin traffic
nodes.rationale: The insecure-by-default trap is inverted: an unconfigured deployment is visibly broken (empty allow_origins) rather than invisibly unsafe ("*"). tracing.endpoint: "" applies the same idea from the other side — empty means a no-op tracer so the app still runs.
nodes.norm_label: cors default rejects all cross-origin traffic

nodes.label: Escape-safe DSN assembly (net/url, FormatDSN)
nodes.rationale: Config carries discrete typed fields rather than a single DATABASE_URL, and the DSN is built with url.UserPassword + net.JoinHostPort (or mysql.Config.FormatDSN) because a raw fmt.Sprintf corrupts the URL the moment a password contains @ : / ? # or a space — the single most common way a generated project breaks on a rotated password.

nodes.label: Thin client wrapper types (cache.Client, search.Client)
nodes.rationale: Embedding redis.UniversalClient makes single/sentinel/cluster a CONFIG choice rather than a code change — every caller depends on *cache.Client while the full redis API stays available without re-exporting methods.

nodes.label: Kafka consumer group with OffsetOldest
nodes.rationale: OffsetOldest only applies to a group with no committed offsets, so a fresh deployment replays history instead of silently skipping messages published before it started. Group membership (not manual partition assignment) is what makes replicas rebalance. The factory fails fast on a missing consumer_group_id and does no consuming, which is what keeps it infrastructure.

nodes.label: Shutdown context rooted at context.Background()
nodes.rationale: By the time cleanup runs the request-lifecycle ctx is already SIGINT-cancelled; deriving the shutdown ctx from it collapses ShutdownTimeout to zero and kills every in-flight request mid-response. Rooting at Background() is what makes shutdown_timeout: 10s mean anything.

nodes.label: callerSkip — wrapper frames vs caller reporting
nodes.rationale: Wrapping a logger usually breaks its caller field: without counting the emit -> Logger.<Level> -> real call site frames, every line reports the wrapper as the source. A new method that calls emit at a different depth must change callerSkip with it.
nodes.norm_label: callerskip — wrapper frames vs caller reporting

nodes.label: RS256 rather than HS256 for access tokens
nodes.rationale: With a shared HMAC secret every service that can VERIFY a token can also FORGE one. Asymmetric keys mean only the issuer holds the signing key, and rotation is: publish the new public key fleet-wide, then start signing. Keys are base64 PEM so they survive single-line env vars and are parsed once at startup. The package is jwtsec, not jwt, to avoid colliding with golang-jwt.
nodes.norm_label: rs256 rather than hs256 for access tokens

nodes.label: Token verification returns a generic 401, reason logged by severity
nodes.rationale: Telling a caller WHY their token failed (expired vs bad signature) is an oracle, so the distinction is preserved in logs instead — and triaged: routine rejections (expired, malformed client garbage) go to Debug because at scale they are constant noise, while an invalid signature goes to Warn because it means either fleet key drift or a forged token. Anything unrecognised is treated as anomalous so new failure modes surface as Warn.
nodes.norm_label: token verification returns a generic 401, reason logged by severity

nodes.label: Bcrypt cost clamped, never errored
nodes.rationale: Clamping an out-of-range BCRYPT_COST to DefaultCost yields a safe value instead of a boot failure — and, critically, never yields cost 0. Verify collapses every mismatch to ErrUnauthorized, which is what lets Login return a uniform InvalidCredentials.

nodes.label: No-op tracer still installs the propagator
nodes.rationale: With an empty endpoint the SDK is skipped but the propagator is still set, so inbound traceparent headers keep flowing — running one hop without a collector doesn't break a distributed trace. Shutdown flushes pending spans; skipping it loses the last spans before exit.
nodes.norm_label: no-op tracer still installs the propagator

nodes.label: Shared packages (pkg/)
nodes.rationale: Cross-cutting utilities with no layer affiliation. Nothing here imports internal/ and nothing imports a framework — that rule is what makes pkg/ legitimate rather than a dumping ground.

nodes.label: pkg/errors — AppError with a caller-info trace
nodes.rationale: Three deliberate non-goals: no stack dumps (a wrap trail is cheaper and more readable), no status codes passed to Wrap (classification happens where the error originates), and no language in business code (translation happens at the boundary). Args and Err are json:"-" so user data and diagnostics never reach the client.
nodes.norm_label: pkg/errors — apperror with a caller-info trace

nodes.label: Sentinels + std re-exports (one errors import)
nodes.rationale: Re-exporting New/Is/As/Unwrap/Join means a file needs one errors import, not two — which is why repositories alias the stdlib as stderrors only when they need a driver sentinel. The sentinels are the adapter->usecase vocabulary.

nodes.label: Classify once, at the layer that knows what went wrong
nodes.rationale: Wrap/Wrapf append a frame but preserve Code/Message/Locale/Args, so twelve layers of Wrapf on a 404 still produce a 404. Wrap(nil) returns nil so `return errors.Wrap(err, ...)` is safe unconditionally. classify() is always locale-coded, so an unclassified third-party error can never leak its raw text to a client.
nodes.norm_label: classify once, at the layer that knows what went wrong

nodes.label: WithCause — diagnostics without changing classification
nodes.rationale: The cause is never rendered to the client; it surfaces only in the access log's app_err/app_trace, so an otherwise-opaque generic 4xx stays traceable by request_id.

nodes.label: Frame trail instead of a stack dump
nodes.rationale: A frame is runtime.Caller only — no full-stack walk or symbolization. You get the path the error took through YOUR layers, which is the part you actually read, and shortFile matches the logger's caller format so a trace entry and a log caller field read the same way.
nodes.norm_label: frame trail instead of a stack dump

nodes.label: localeHTTPStatus — one table, one status per code
nodes.rationale: Both construction paths (L() and classify()) read the same table, so a code has exactly one status and the two paths cannot drift. Being framework-free, gRPC and worker transports reuse it without a second mapping. A code absent from the table silently resolves to 500, so adding a locale code means adding a row.
nodes.norm_label: localehttpstatus — one table, one status per code

nodes.label: The AppError context stash (mutable slot in ctx)
nodes.rationale: The response is written after the middleware's outbound ctx has been observed, and contexts are immutable, so a pointer-to-struct slot is a mutable channel UPWARD. It is the only place the codebase does this, and it is what buys 'handlers never log'. StashAppError no-ops when the slot is absent so tests and background contexts are safe.
nodes.norm_label: the apperror context stash (mutable slot in ctx)

nodes.label: errors.LogFields — same field names without middleware
nodes.rationale: The worker has no access-log middleware to fold cause and trace in for it, so it renders the same app_code/app_err/app_trace/app_locale keys by hand — one log query shape then works across HTTP and worker logs.
nodes.norm_label: errors.logfields — same field names without middleware

nodes.label: pkg/locale — codes and translations, no status
nodes.rationale: Division of labour: codes and text here, HTTP status in pkg/errors — keeping the status table out is what lets a non-HTTP transport use the same codes. LocaleError stores Args raw so the same error renders in any language; Translate falls back language->English then code->English then 'unknown error: %d', so a half-translated language degrades per-string.
nodes.norm_label: pkg/locale — codes and translations, no status

nodes.label: Error codes are negative ints banded by feature
nodes.rationale: Negative so they cannot be confused with an HTTP status in a response body, and banded (General -1000s, User -1100s) so a new feature claims a range instead of appending to a flat list.
nodes.norm_label: error codes are negative ints banded by feature

nodes.label: Translations register explicitly (no init())
nodes.rationale: NewMapping() is called once at startup so registration order is explicit and testable; a project that forgets it serves 'unknown error: -1100'.

nodes.label: The single response envelope (success/data/error/meta/requestId)
nodes.rationale: Surfacing requestId in the body turns a user's screenshot into a complete server-side replay: grepping that request_id replays every line the request produced, with caller file:line. RequestIDFrom lives in pkg/httputil so inner layers can read it without importing transport.

nodes.label: Two pagination metas, two audiences
nodes.rationale: CursorMeta exposes no totals on purpose — counting every match defeats keyset paging, which is stable under concurrent inserts and cheap at depth. PageMeta's TotalPage/TotalRecord need a COUNT query, so it is reserved for back-office lists. NewPageMeta returns 0 rather than dividing by zero.

nodes.label: ErrorResponseFromApp — locale code becomes the client code
nodes.rationale: The HTTP status says category (404) while error.code says reason (-1100 UserNotFound vs -1003 RecordNotFound), so a client branches on the specific code without string matching. A nil app still produces a valid translated envelope, so a caller bug can't emit garbage.
nodes.norm_label: errorresponsefromapp — locale code becomes the client code

nodes.label: pkg/observability.Logger port
nodes.rationale: The port lives in pkg/ and the implementation in internal/infrastructure/logger — that inversion is what lets a usecase log without importing infrastructure. Tracing and metrics are deliberately NOT modelled as ports: the OTel package-level APIs plus ctx-threaded span context already serve as the seam.

nodes.label: Reserved log field names (time, level, caller, message)
nodes.rationale: Reusing one emits a duplicate JSON field, which most log pipelines resolve unpredictably. The human-readable text is the msg argument and must never also be passed as a kv.
nodes.norm_label: reserved log field names (time, level, caller, message)

nodes.label: pkg/logctx — request-scoped logger through context
nodes.rationale: From() never returns nil (it falls back to a nop logger), which is why logctx.From(ctx).Warn(...) appears inline with no guard across adapters and usecases. The package creates no loggers and depends only on the port, keeping the direction usecase -> logctx -> observability.

nodes.label: DI and entry points
nodes.rationale: main.go -> cmd.Execute() -> cobra root -> per-transport subcommand -> internal/app lifecycle -> di.Initialize*. Wire and fx produce identical Initialize* signatures so internal/app is byte-for-byte the same either way.

nodes.label: One binary, one subcommand per transport
nodes.rationale: locale.NewMapping() is called in Execute() — not in an init() and not in DI — so translations register exactly once before any subcommand runs, and a CLI subcommand that never builds the DI graph still gets them.
nodes.norm_label: one binary, one subcommand per transport

nodes.label: RunE, not Run (never os.Exit inside a command)
nodes.rationale: Returning the error lets cobra print it and Execute set the exit code; calling os.Exit(1) inside the command would skip every pending defer, including the DI cleanup that closes the pool and flushes spans.
nodes.norm_label: rune, not run (never os.exit inside a command)

nodes.label: internal/app lifecycle (signal, goroutine, buffered errChan)
nodes.rationale: signal.NotifyContext owns shutdown; Start() runs in a goroutine so the function can select on both the signal and a startup failure (a blocking Listen in the main goroutine can't observe SIGTERM); http.ErrServerClosed is not an error or every clean stop exits non-zero; errChan is buffered size 1 so the goroutine can't leak blocking on a send after select returned; defer cleanup() is registered immediately after Initialize* succeeds so every return path runs it.

nodes.label: App bundle holds Tracer to keep the flush hook alive
nodes.rationale: A DI graph only builds what the requested type transitively needs; with nothing referencing the tracer the tracing provider — and its cleanup hook — would be pruned and the last spans before exit lost. The entry point never reads the field; listing it is what forces the flush. Conversely WorkerApp omitting HTTPServer is what keeps HTTP providers out of the worker binary.
nodes.norm_label: app bundle holds tracer to keep the flush hook alive

nodes.label: provideRegistrars / provideWorkerHandlers are the extension points
nodes.rationale: Adding a feature means adding its constructor to a set and its instance to one of these slices; slice order determines mount order, not the prefix string. provideTracingConfig exists so infrastructure/tracing can keep its own neutral Config and avoid a compile-time dep on config.
nodes.norm_label: provideregistrars / provideworkerhandlers are the extension points

nodes.label: Layered, unexported wire provider sets
nodes.rationale: Mode-specific sets are not cosmetic: a worker project has no JWT keys configured and NewTokenService errors on a missing public key, so keeping it out of workerInfraSet means the worker never constructs it. All sets are unexported because nothing outside di composes them. The wireinject build tag also means go vet alone can't validate wire.go — which is why nova's test matrix stubs wire_gen.go.

nodes.label: wire.FieldsOf projects sub-configs
nodes.rationale: This is the mechanism that lets every constructor take the sub-struct it actually reads instead of the whole *Config; nested projection (HTTP -> LoginRateLimit) works the same way.

nodes.label: wire.Bind is where dependency inversion is executed
nodes.rationale: Every wire.Bind is one arrow in the layer diagram: the usecase names domain.UserRepository and this line is the only place that says 'postgres'. Swapping in the Redis cache decorator changes exactly one of them. Editing sets without re-running `wire ./...` changes nothing about the built binary — a confusing failure mode.
nodes.norm_label: wire.bind is where dependency inversion is executed

nodes.label: fx as a drop-in for Wire (identical Initialize* signatures)
nodes.rationale: One fx.Option module per Wire set, fx.Populate as the analogue of wire.Struct (populating tracer for the same flush reason), and fx_provider.go adapting each (instance, cleanup, error) constructor into an OnStop hook — so the two engines converge on the same cleanup semantics and the app layer never learns which built the graph. fx.NopLogger keeps the app's structured logs the only output.
nodes.norm_label: fx as a drop-in for wire (identical initialize* signatures)

nodes.label: Cleanups composed in reverse construction order
nodes.rationale: Reverse order is correctness, not tidiness: the server stops accepting requests BEFORE the pool it depends on closes, so no in-flight request meets a closed pool. You get it for free only if every constructor that owns a resource returns its cleanup — one that closes nothing leaks it and no test will tell you.
nodes.norm_label: cleanups composed in reverse construction order

nodes.label: Adding a feature — the full checklist
nodes.rationale: Steps 5-6 (wire.go sets, provideRegistrars) are the ones people forget, and their failure modes differ: skip the set and wire fails to generate; skip the slice and everything compiles but the routes are never mounted.
nodes.norm_label: adding a feature — the full checklist

nodes.label: Makefile targets (composed, self-documenting)
nodes.rationale: test runs -race because the alternative is finding the race in production; lint chains sqlfluff so hand-written SQL is held to the same bar; gen expands to only the generators the project has, so a --di=fx --query=none project's gen is a no-op rather than an error; wire-gen deletes wire_gen.go first because a stale generated file that still compiles is worse than a missing one; migrate-* read $MIGRATE_DATABASE_URL because migration tooling runs outside the app. There is deliberately no make build/run — running means choosing a subcommand and make would have to guess.

nodes.label: pre-commit hook: format, then fail if formatting changed anything
nodes.rationale: A hook that mutates the commit you're making is how surprising diffs land in a PR, so it stops and asks you to review and stage the reformatting. It is opt-in via `make setup` because a hook that installs itself is hostile, and the generator must render it 0o700 — git silently skips a non-executable hook, so one without +x looks installed and does nothing.
nodes.norm_label: pre-commit hook: format, then fail if formatting changed anything

nodes.label: Two-stage Dockerfile, non-root static binary
nodes.rationale: go.mod/go.sum copied before the source so go mod download is a cached layer; CGO_ENABLED=0 for a static binary; -ldflags="-w -s" strips DWARF and symbols; USER app because running as root is the default and the wrong default; ca-certificates + tzdata installed explicitly because a static Go binary has neither and their absence shows up as TLS failures and UTC-only timestamps. ENTRYPOINT/CMD are split so `docker run img worker` overrides only the subcommand.

nodes.label: Generated code is committed, not generated in the image
nodes.rationale: Keeps the build hermetic — no wire/sqlc in the builder stage, no network beyond module download — and makes the generated DI graph reviewable in a PR.
nodes.norm_label: generated code is committed, not generated in the image

nodes.label: Container healthcheck probes /readyz, not /healthz
nodes.rationale: A container that is up but can't reach its database should not be routed traffic; start-period=10s gives the app time to dial dependencies on cold boot. EXPOSE and the healthcheck are transport-gated, so a worker image declares neither.

nodes.label: Every compose limit is an env var with a default
nodes.rationale: A benchmark sweep becomes a shell loop over one variable and every run is reproducible because the ceiling is explicit rather than 'whatever the host had free'. Requires Compose V2 — V1 ignores deploy.resources.limits outside swarm. environment overriding env_file is what lets one .env serve both host-side runs (localhost) and in-network runs (service names).
nodes.norm_label: every compose limit is an env var with a default

nodes.label: Dependencies wait for health, not for start
nodes.rationale: Without condition: service_healthy the app dials a still-booting database, fails, and exits — the single most common 'compose doesn't work' report. Host ports are published anyway so host tooling (migrate, k6, kafka CLI) hits the same stack; Kafka runs KRaft with dual listeners for exactly that.
nodes.norm_label: dependencies wait for health, not for start

nodes.label: CI: lint + tidy + test gate build
nodes.rationale: The tidy job (go mod tidy then git diff --exit-code) is the one people leave out and regret: an untidy go.mod breaks other people's builds in ways that look unrelated to the PR that caused it. test uses service containers mirroring compose, with throwaway committed base64 PEM JWT fixtures because NewTokenService parses keys at startup and would fail the whole test binary without them. permissions: contents: read scopes the token to the minimum.
nodes.norm_label: ci: lint + tidy + test gate build

nodes.label: .env.example holds only secrets and per-deploy endpoints
nodes.rationale: Tuning is reviewed in code (base.yaml + <APP_ENV>.yaml), secrets are injected. Notable entries: JWT keys with generation commands and a note that only the issuer sets the private key; CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS empty with 'production MUST set this, never *'; discrete DB fields rather than DATABASE_URL; MIGRATE_DATABASE_URL flagged as tooling-only, not read by the Go config.
nodes.norm_label: .env.example holds only secrets and per-deploy endpoints

nodes.label: Cross-cutting features every generated project ships
nodes.rationale: Templates must never omit these — adding a new HTTP framework variant means re-implementing the list for that framework, not removing items.
nodes.norm_label: cross-cutting features every generated project ships

nodes.label: Everything rides on context.Context
nodes.rationale: Two rules keep it from being a global-variable bag: the key type is always an unexported struct{} so no package can collide or read the value without the accessor, and the accessors live with the VALUE not the setter — pkg/locale owns WithLanguage/LanguageFromContext even though only middleware sets it, which is what lets pkg/httputil read the language without importing transport.

nodes.label: Log once, at the boundary
nodes.rationale: One line per failed request means error-rate alerting counts requests, not layers; the frame trail replaces the stack with the path through your own code; correlation is free because request_id/trace_id are on the scoped logger and requestId in the body is the user's handle. The three exceptions are all 'the error is being swallowed here, so it must be logged here': best-effort publish, cache read/refill failures, panic recovery.

nodes.label: Classify at the origin, translate at the edge
nodes.rationale: The status is decided where the error is created from one table, so Wrapf at ten layers can't turn a 409 into a 500; the language is decided at the boundary so business code never names one; args travel raw so the same error renders in any language. Because the table is framework-free a gRPC or worker transport reuses the classification.
nodes.norm_label: classify at the origin, translate at the edge

nodes.label: Each component owns its shutdown
nodes.rationale: The cost to internalize: a constructor that acquires a resource and doesn't return a cleanup leaks it and nothing will tell you. The benefit: adding a dependency can't break shutdown ordering.

nodes.label: Security posture (spread across layers by design)
nodes.rationale: Collected in one table because each measure is documented at its source: bcrypt with clamped cost, credentials never in a DTO/cache/index, uniform 401 AND uniform timing, RS256 so only the issuer can sign, generic 401 with the reason logged, per-IP bucket on /login only, explicit CORS origins, generic 400 with the field cause logged, c.Path() so query strings never reach logs, env-only JWT keys, sqlc prepared statements, escape-safe DSN, non-root container.
nodes.norm_label: security posture (spread across layers by design)

nodes.label: Observability at a glance (log -> trace -> replay)
nodes.rationale: Three properties: trace_id on every line makes a log search jump to Jaeger/Tempo; the response body's requestId turns a user report into a full replay; probes and OPTIONS emit no line and a plain validation 400 omits app_err/app_trace, so client-driven noise doesn't move error-rate alerts.
nodes.norm_label: observability at a glance (log -> trace -> replay)

nodes.label: What is deliberately absent
nodes.rationale: Stated explicitly so nobody assumes coverage: no /metrics, no general rate limiter (global shedding belongs upstream), no outbox (publishing is best-effort-with-logging), no refresh tokens, no authorization (Auth establishes who, not what they may do), gRPC is a stub, transport/cronjob + cmd/cron.go exist as templates but are not wired into buildFileList.

nodes.label: False calls edges from bare-symbol resolution
nodes.rationale: The AST pass resolved calls edges by bare symbol name, so every unqualified `New(` was wired to generator.New. Verified false edges: renderTemplateString -> template.New, generateSQLCRepository -> errors.New, the two identical-template tests -> template.New, validateComponent -> errors.New. Consequence: three of the six communities New() appeared to bridge (sqlc Repository Code-Gen, Component Generator Tests, CLI Command Wiring) are not connected to it at all, and its 0.254 betweenness is inflated.
nodes.norm_label: false calls edges from bare-symbol resolution

nodes.label: generator.New() as the up-front validation gate
nodes.rationale: New() is a 13-line validation gate before any template path is resolved: three whitelist checks (frameworks, databases, DI), then a FuncMap and the struct — no I/O, no file list. It is the only cheap place to reject an unsupported option, which is why the CLI wants the early error, the matrix tests want a fast assertion point that renders nothing, and the docs want one function to name for up-front rejection. Louvain even assigned New() to the test-matrix community rather than its own file's, because 15 verified test edges outweigh its 3 same-package edges.
nodes.norm_label: generator.new() as the up-front validation gate

nodes.label: Commit graphify-out so a clone starts with the map
nodes.rationale: graph.json, GRAPH_REPORT.md, graph.html and manifest.json are tracked in git so a teammate can query the graph immediately after cloning; first-time setup is only installing the tool, never rebuilding the graph. cost.json (per-machine token tally) and cache/ stay ignored.
nodes.norm_label: commit graphify-out so a clone starts with the map

nodes.label: Code is AST-parsed locally, so no API key is required
nodes.rationale: tree-sitter parsing is deterministic and runs locally, so Go code costs no tokens. Only docs, PDFs and images reach semantic extraction, which is why the setup guide lists the API key as optional step 5 rather than a prerequisite.
nodes.norm_label: code is ast-parsed locally, so no api key is required

nodes.label: EXTRACTED vs INFERRED edge tagging makes the graph auditable
nodes.rationale: every edge records whether it was explicit in the source or resolved by graphify, so a reader can tell derived structure from asserted structure instead of trusting the whole graph equally.
nodes.norm_label: extracted vs inferred edge tagging makes the graph auditable

nodes.label: Git hooks are per-developer, not shared through the repo
nodes.rationale: hooks live in .git/hooks/ which git never tracks, so committing the graph does not distribute the rebuild automation. Every developer runs `graphify hook install` themselves, and re-runs it after reinstalling graphify because the hook pins an interpreter path at install time.
nodes.norm_label: git hooks are per-developer, not shared through the repo

nodes.label: Post-commit rebuild runs detached and code-only
nodes.rationale: the hook re-runs AST extraction on changed files in a background process so `git commit` returns immediately and costs nothing. Because it is code-only, markdown edits are invisible to it and need an explicit `--update`.
nodes.norm_label: post-commit rebuild runs detached and code-only

nodes.label: Shrink guard refuses to overwrite graph.json with fewer nodes
nodes.rationale: a half-broken extraction would otherwise silently replace a good graph, so a smaller result is rejected by default. An intentional shrink after deleting code needs --force or GRAPHIFY_FORCE=1.
nodes.norm_label: shrink guard refuses to overwrite graph.json with fewer nodes

nodes.label: Tracked sidecars hold machine-absolute paths
nodes.rationale: .graphify_python and .graphify_root record absolute paths from whoever built the graph, so they are wrong on every other clone. The interpreter path is guarded by an executable probe and falls through harmlessly, but .graphify_root is read as the scan root by the hook's background rebuild, which can then target a directory that does not exist. Both should be gitignored and regenerated locally.

nodes.label: Gemini key is optional; the host assistant is the fallback extractor
nodes.rationale: semantic extraction uses Gemini when GEMINI_API_KEY or GOOGLE_API_KEY is set and otherwise falls back to the assistant session itself, so setup never blocks on obtaining a key.
nodes.norm_label: gemini key is optional; the host assistant is the fallback extractor

nodes.label: Tracking graph.json trades clone-time value for merge conflicts
nodes.rationale: committing the graph means concurrent branches collide on graph.json. Either side can be taken and rebuilt by the hook, or graphify's union merge driver resolves it, because the file is regenerable output rather than authored source.
nodes.norm_label: tracking graph.json trades clone-time value for merge conflicts

nodes.label: Query the graph instead of reading raw files
nodes.rationale: with graph.json present the assistant answers architecture questions by traversal (query, path, explain, affected) rather than grepping; `graphify claude install` makes that preference explicit per developer instead of committing it to CLAUDE.md.
nodes.norm_label: query the graph instead of reading raw files

nodes.label: README advertises the committed knowledge graph
nodes.rationale: the Development section points at graphify-out/ and GRAPHIFY.md so the graph is discoverable from the front door; the setup detail lives in GRAPHIFY.md to keep docs/ scoped to the generated project's design reference.
nodes.norm_label: readme advertises the committed knowledge graph

nodes.label: A flag-driven `nova new` must pass --transport
nodes.rationale: any flag skips the prompts entirely, so omitting --transport in a non-interactive run generates a project with no entry point.

nodes.label: sqlc repository generation requires the entity to exist first
nodes.rationale: the entity's fields drive the migration columns, sqlc query, typed impl and mapper, so `nova add repository` errors without it. Unsupported field types are skipped with a warning so the emitted code always compiles.
nodes.norm_label: sqlc repository generation requires the entity to exist first

nodes.label: nova.yaml describes layout for non-nova projects
nodes.rationale: `add` resolves each component's destination from nova.yaml, with per-key fallback to nova's defaults, so projects generated by `nova new` need no file and foreign layouts are supported without changing the generator.
nodes.norm_label: nova.yaml describes layout for non-nova projects

nodes.label: Interfaces live where the consumer is
nodes.rationale: repository ports sit in domain/ because use cases call them, and framework-specific helpers sit under their transport; inner layers never import outer ones.
nodes.norm_label: interfaces live where the consumer is

nodes.label: Worker DI scaffold writes only symbols the project lacks
nodes.rationale: WorkerApp and InitializeWorker are emitted only when the di package does not already declare them, so a worker-enabled project is left untouched and repeat runs never duplicate; shared transport files are likewise written only when absent, so a second `add worker` appends just its feature handler.
nodes.norm_label: worker di scaffold writes only symbols the project lacks
